summary: Grenada is an island nation in the south-eastern Caribbean, known as the "Isle of Spice" for its abundant nutmeg and other spices, and it became independent from Britain in 1974.

ranking.name: Protestant Christianity
ranking.description: After the Treaty of Paris of 1763 Grenada was ceded by France to Britain, British rule was established in 1783, and the Anglican Church became the official church of the colony, with Methodists, Presbyterians and others introduced afterward. From the 20th century the Seventh-day Adventists and Pentecostal churches grew rapidly, making the Protestant denominations together the largest religious group.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1649 the French came from Martinique to Grenada, conquered the indigenous Kalinago (Island Caribs), and established sugar and cocoa plantations, and Catholicism was introduced with them. Although the British made the Anglican Church the official church after taking over, the French-descended residents and their descendants of African slaves had already formed a solid Catholic community, and Catholic schools still play an important role in education today.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are mostly young people in towns, related to the spread of education, study abroad and the influence of internet culture. Because the church is still important in community life, the proportion is not high.

ranking.name: Rastafari
ranking.description: Rastafari originated in Jamaica in the 1930s and was brought to Grenada in the 1970s with reggae music, attracting some young people seeking an African identity. During the revolution led by Maurice Bishop in 1979, some Rastafarians took part, but the followers have always been a minority.

religion.background: Grenada was originally inhabited by the Kalinago; when the French army conquered the island in 1651, many Kalinago leapt from a cliff at Sauteurs in the north to avoid capture, and the indigenous beliefs disappeared with them. French colonization brought Catholicism, and British rule after 1763 brought the Anglican Church and various Protestant denominations, and the African slaves who were trafficked here accepted Christianity within the two colonial cultures. After independence in 1974 there has been religious freedom; today Protestants and Catholics together make up more than eighty percent, with small numbers of Hindus and Muslims descended from Indian indentured laborers.

ranking.name: Grenadian Creole English
ranking.description: Grenadian Creole English formed on the plantations during British colonial rule, combining English vocabulary with grammatical features of West African languages and also retaining a number of French loanwords. It is the language that the vast majority of Grenadians use at home and in daily life, forming a continuum with Standard English.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: After Grenada came under British rule in 1763, English became the language of administration, law and schools, and after independence in 1974 it remains the sole official language. Standard English is used on formal occasions, in the media and in education, but relatively few people have it as a first language.

ranking.name: Grenadian Creole French
ranking.description: During French rule in 1649–1763 a French-based Creole (Patois) formed on the plantations. After the British took over, English gradually replaced it, and in the 20th century only elderly people in rural areas still used it; it is now nearly extinct and survives only in traces in some place names and words, such as the place names Grenville and Sauteurs.

language.history: The language of Grenada's indigenous Kalinago disappeared with the French conquest. From the mid-17th century French colonization made French Creole the common language of the plantations, and after the island came under British rule in 1763, English gradually replaced French and an English-based Creole formed. The arrival of Indian indentured laborers in the mid-19th century also brought a small number of Indian words. Today English is the official language, Creole English is the everyday spoken language, and French Creole has almost died out.

ranking.name: Oil down
ranking.description: Breadfruit, salted meat, chicken, dumplings and callaloo leaves are put into coconut milk, seasoned with turmeric and cooked slowly until the coconut milk is completely absorbed.
ranking.history: The name comes from the cooking process: the coconut milk is slowly absorbed by the ingredients, leaving at the end only a layer of oil at the bottom of the pot (oil down). Breadfruit is a crop that Captain Bligh carried from the Pacific to the Caribbean in 1793, and salted meat was a ration imported for slaves in the colonial period, so this dish condenses Grenada's colonial history. It is regarded as Grenada's national dish and is often cooked collectively in big pots over wood fires at beaches or community gatherings, a symbol of sharing and togetherness.

ranking.name: Callaloo
ranking.description: A thick green soup stewed from dasheen (taro) leaves, okra, coconut milk and spices, sometimes with crab or salted meat added.
ranking.history: This kind of leafy green soup originates in West Africa, and the slaves trafficked to the Caribbean recreated their homeland's stewed greens with the dasheen leaves and okra available locally. In Grenada, callaloo also refers to the dasheen leaves themselves, which are often added to dishes such as oil down. It is a common soup at Sunday family lunches and symbolizes the food tradition of Afro-Caribbean people.

ranking.name: Nutmeg
ranking.description: Nutmeg is Grenada's most famous spice; the kernel is ground and used in desserts, drinks and sauces, while the red aril is made into the spice mace.
ranking.history: Nutmeg is native to the Banda Islands of Indonesia and was introduced to Grenada by the British in the mid-19th century (generally said to be 1843), quickly becoming the main cash crop and earning Grenada the name "Isle of Spice"; at one time it was the world's second-largest nutmeg producer. At independence in 1974 nutmeg was depicted on the national flag. In 2004 Hurricane Ivan destroyed most of the nutmeg trees, severely damaging the local economy. Today the island still has many jams, syrups and rums made with nutmeg.

ranking.name: Bake (fried bread)
ranking.description: Flour, baking powder, salt and water are kneaded into a dough, pressed into small rounds and fried or baked, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten with salt fish for breakfast.
ranking.history: Bakes are linked to the flour imported during British colonial rule, when colonial residents used cheap imported flour to make cakes that could quickly fill the stomach. Its most classic way of eating is with salt fish for breakfast, and it is also often taken to school or work as a packed meal. This simple food is common across the English-speaking Caribbean islands and is part of Grenadians' everyday diet.

ranking.name: Roti
ranking.description: A large thin flatbread made of flour, filled with curried chicken, potato or chickpeas, and folded into a square or rolled up like a wrap to eat.
ranking.history: From 1857 the British colonial government, to supplement the plantation labor force after the abolition of slavery, brought indentured laborers from India to Grenada, and they brought roti and curry. Although people of Indian descent are not a high proportion of Grenada's population, roti has become integrated into the local diet and is a common lunch at fast-food shops and in homes, reflecting the diverse immigration history of the Caribbean.
